recall.q: Mice given psilocybin under anesthesia still became more social. What does that suggest about the trip, and which mice did not benefit?
recall.a: In these mice, the felt trip was not needed. The effect seemed to come from the drug acting on the 5HT2A receptor. Normal mice got no social boost, so the drug helped only mice whose social behavior was out of balance.

cards.title: India may need to import sugar for a second year
cards.body: For nearly ten years, India made more sugar than it used. Last season that ended, and India had to import sugar. Industry executives now expect a second year of imports.

sections.text:
In the 2025-26 season, output fell and sugar prices at home hit record highs.

Now Maharashtra and Karnataka, two big cane-growing states, have had too little rain for a long time. Reservoir water is also being kept for drinking instead of going to farms. Executives expect both problems to lower the sugar content of the cane crushed from October. Less sugar in each stalk means less sugar from the same harvest.

sections.label: The numbers
items: India's rank among sugar producers: 2nd in the world
Years India made more sugar than it used: nearly 10
When crushing of the new cane starts: October

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.text: One bad year can be bad luck. Two in a row suggests the long surplus may be ending. Weak rain and short water supply now hit both farm output and what people pay for food.

sections.label: Watch next
sections.text: How much sugar the cane gives once crushing starts in October. That will show if the executives are right.

recall.q: Why do executives expect India to import sugar again, and what will the problem do to the cane?
recall.a: Maharashtra and Karnataka have had too little rain for a long time, and reservoir water is being kept for drinking, not farms. This is expected to lower the sugar content of cane crushed from October, so the same harvest gives less sugar.

cards.title: Higher weight tied to a jumpier brain reward signal
cards.body: Most research asks how strongly the brain responds to food. This study asked a different question: how steady is that response? In 79 women, higher body weight went with a reward signal that jumped up and down from one moment to the next.
cards.evidence: single study · n=79 women (59 scanned) · grip task + fMRI + self-report

sections.text:
The prize is a small snack, and the price is a squeeze. Each woman in this study held a grip device and pressed it to win food or money. The task was set to her own top strength, so the effort felt the same for everyone, fit or not.

One major theory of overeating says that eating very rewarding food again and again makes the brain's wanting system more sensitive. Food cues then set off bigger cravings. But hunger and fullness rise and fall all day. If eating for pleasure keeps winning over the body's fullness signal, the brain's response to food might not grow stronger. It might grow unstable. So a team at the University of Tübingen in Germany, led by Nils B. Kroemer, measured how much that signal jumps around.

They recruited 79 women. 35 had binge eating disorder: repeated episodes of eating large amounts while feeling out of control. 21 had a milder, less frequent form, and 23 had no binge eating. The groups had a similar average body mass index (BMI, a weight-for-height score). That let the team separate the effect of the disorder from the effect of weight.

After each round, the women rated how much they wanted the prize. Sometimes the screen showed how hard they had to squeeze. Sometimes it was hidden. Points later became real cash or real snack calories. Women with binge eating disorder gave food ratings that swung widely from round to round, most of all when the effort was hidden. Their ratings for money did not swing. And their squeezing stayed steady while their wanting jumped. The researchers suggest these women may rely on outside cues or habit to decide how hard to work.

Next, 59 women came back after fasting overnight and did the task inside an fMRI scanner. This machine tracks blood flow as an indirect sign of brain activity. The team looked at the moment a prize appeared, before any squeezing began. They studied two areas. The nucleus accumbens, deep in the brain, handles reward and wanting. The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, near the front, handles self-control and weighing costs.

Here the pattern followed weight, not diagnosis. Women with higher BMI had more up-and-down signals in both areas. Women who often eat without restraint (a standard questionnaire calls this disinhibited eating) also had a jumpier nucleus accumbens. Brain areas that do not handle reward showed no such pattern, so this was not just general noise. Women with binge eating disorder showed slightly more swing than the control group, but the difference was not statistically significant. It could be chance.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: Only women took part, and the study could not check the effect of sex hormones, which shape eating and reward. The lab kept meal timing and mood steady, but real binges are often set off by changing emotions and body states. Nobody's actual eating was measured. The study measured only how hard they would work for food and how their brain reacted while waiting for it. Finally, heavier people sometimes move a little more in scanners, and small head movements can look like jumpy brain activity. The team corrected for this with mathematical models, but some leftover effect is possible.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The problem may not be a craving that is too loud, but a signal that will not hold still.

recall.q: In the brain scans, what went with a jumpier reward signal: the binge eating diagnosis, or something else?
recall.a: Mostly higher BMI, plus a habit of eating without restraint. Women with binge eating disorder showed only a small increase that was not significant. Their clear difference showed up elsewhere: their conscious wanting for food swung widely from round to round.
